description:
HttpCrlFetcher, HttpOcspFetcher, AsyncHttpCrlFetcher, AsyncHttpOcspFetcher,
CachedHttpCrlFetcher, and CachedHttpOcspFetcher all take \`now_unix: u64\` at
construction (lib.rs:343, lib.rs:389, async_fetcher.rs:165, async_fetcher.rs:198)
and freeze it for the lifetime of the value. The rustdoc on each \`new()\`
describes the argument as \"current time as seconds since the Unix epoch\" with
no warning that the value is captured, not re-read.

Caller contract gap: a caller who builds the fetcher once at startup and reuses
it across requests gets a validator that never advances. Validity-period
checks, CRL freshness, OCSP \`nextUpdate\` enforcement all evaluate against
whatever wall-clock the caller passed weeks ago. Two failure modes follow:

1. Long-uptime services will accept revoked certs whose CRL has rotated past
   the captured \`now_unix\`.
2. Callers who notice and reconstruct the fetcher on every \`check_revocation\`
   call rebuild the whole \`F + V\` state per check (clones, agent re-use lost,
   cache pointer churn).

The rustdoc must either:

- Document that \`now_unix\` is a per-invocation parameter and require the
  caller to reconstruct the fetcher on every check; OR
- Accept a \`time_source: impl Fn() -> u64\` callback so the validator can
  re-read at \`check_revocation\` time without forcing reconstruction.

The latter is the strictly more flexible contract. Either way, the silent
freezing-of-time is undocumented and the doc comment misleads readers.
title: now_unix captured at construction; long-lived fetchers validate against stale time
